```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(classInt)

#course data (read once for the whole page)
acs_tract_nc <- st_read("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jucardwell/geog391/main/data/nc_tract_acs_2023.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
triangle <- acs_tract_nc |> filter(COUNTYFP %in% c("135", "183", "063"))
meck <- acs_tract_nc |> filter(COUNTYFP == "119")

#numbers quoted in the text below come from here, so they stay right if the data changes
fmt <- function(x, d = 0) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
```

::: {.plan}
For the first 15 minutes or so, you and your partner will read the walkthrough together and run the code. Then you'll split up for about 25 minutes. Both of you will map median home values in Mecklenburg County, but Partner A will use equal interval classes and Partner B will use quantile classes. In the last 10 minutes you'll compare the two maps and write your answer on an index card.
:::

## Part 1: Walkthrough {#walkthrough}

Run each chunk in your own .Rmd. You will reuse this code in Part 2.

### Step 1: Load the data

::: {.why}
We'll use 2019 to 2023 American Community Survey estimates for the `r nrow(triangle)` census tracts in Orange, Durham and Wake counties. [This file](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1aI2YqE_Tc69ekA48e5jmbyVMXv5uszl-/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=101338019870957132383&rtpof=true&sd=true) explains each variable name.
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)

#ACS census tracts for NC
acs_tract_nc <- st_read("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jucardwell/geog391/main/data/nc_tract_acs_2023.geojson")

#keep Orange (135), Durham (063) and Wake (183) counties
triangle <- acs_tract_nc |> filter(COUNTYFP %in% c("135", "183", "063"))
```

### Step 2: Color and size

::: {.why}
Color (`fill`) works for rates and averages. Size works for counts, like the number of people in a tract.
:::

```{r}
#color
tm_shape(triangle) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "median_age")

#size
tm_shape(triangle) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_symbols(size = "total_pop")
```

### Step 3: Look at the distribution before you classify

::: {.why}
Every choropleth map sorts its values into classes. The right classification depends on the shape of the distribution, so plot a histogram first.
:::

```{r}
ggplot(triangle, aes(x = median_age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Median age", y = "Number of tracts")
```

### Step 4: Choose a classification and a palette

::: {.why}
`style = "equal"` splits the range into classes of the same width, while `style = "quantile"` puts the same number of tracts in each class. Run `cols4all::c4a_gui()` to browse palettes.
:::

```{r}
#equal interval
tm_shape(triangle) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "median_age",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5, values = "bu_pu"))

#quantile
tm_shape(triangle) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "median_age",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "bu_pu"))
```

Other useful styles are `"pretty"` and `"fisher"` (natural breaks).

### Step 5: Finish the map

::: {.why}
`tmap_mode("view")` makes any map interactive, and `tmap_mode("plot")` switches back. A title, some transparency and a basemap make a static map readable on its own.
:::

```{r}
tmap_mode("plot")

tm_shape(triangle) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "median_age", fill_alpha = 0.6,
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "bu_pu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Median age")) +
  tm_title("Median age by census tract") +
  tm_basemap("CartoDB.PositronNoLabels")
```

## Part 2: Partner practice {#partner-practice}

Both partners map `med_house_val`, the median value of owner-occupied homes, for the `r nrow(meck)` census tracts in Mecklenburg County (Charlotte). Partner A uses equal interval classes and Partner B uses quantile classes. Each task tells you in parentheses which walkthrough step to reuse.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#Mecklenburg County tracts (both partners)
meck <- acs_tract_nc |> filter(COUNTYFP == "119")
```

:::: {.partners}
::: {.partner .partner-a}
### Partner A: Equal interval

1. Plot a histogram of `med_house_val`. *(Step 3)*
2. Map it with 5 equal interval classes and a palette you choose. *(Step 4)*
3. Write down the class breaks from the legend. Then count the tracts in each class by using those breaks in `cut()` and `table()`.
4. Add a title, transparency and a basemap. *(Step 5)*

When you finish, bring your class breaks and the number of tracts in each class to Part 3.
:::

::: {.partner .partner-b}
### Partner B: Quantile

1. Plot a histogram of `med_house_val`. *(Step 3)*
2. Map it with 5 quantile classes and a palette you choose. *(Step 4)*
3. Write down the class breaks from the legend. Then count the tracts in each class by using those breaks in `cut()` and `table()`.
4. Add a title, transparency and a basemap. *(Step 5)*

When you finish, bring your class breaks and the number of tracts in each class to Part 3.
:::
::::

## Part 3: Together {#together}

1. Put your two maps side by side and fill in the table.
2. Find a tract that is in the top class on one map but not on the other, and explain why.
3. A housing nonprofit wants a map that shows where homes are least affordable. Decide together which classification it should use, and why.

| Classification | Class breaks | Tracts in each class |
|---|---|---|
| Equal interval (Partner A) | | |
| Quantile (Partner B) | | |

::: {.deliver}
Each pair turns in one index card before leaving. Write both of your names on it, copy the class breaks and counts from the table, and add two or three sentences saying which map the nonprofit should use and why.
:::

## Answer key {#answer-key .answer-key}

```{r key-values, include = FALSE}
x <- meck$med_house_val[!is.na(meck$med_house_val)]
br_eq <- classIntervals(x, n = 5, style = "equal")$brks
br_q <- classIntervals(x, n = 5, style = "quantile")$brks
n_eq <- as.vector(table(cut(x, br_eq, include.lowest = TRUE)))
n_q <- as.vector(table(cut(x, br_q, include.lowest = TRUE)))
brk_text <- function(b) paste0("$", fmt(b), collapse = ", ")
```

| Item | Equal interval (A) | Quantile (B) |
|---|---|---|
| Class breaks | `r brk_text(br_eq)` | `r brk_text(br_q)` |
| Tracts in each class | `r paste(n_eq, collapse = ", ")` | `r paste(n_q, collapse = ", ")` |

Tracts with no estimate: `r sum(is.na(meck$med_house_val))`. tmap may round the legend breaks a little differently, which is fine.

A good card says something like this. Home values are strongly right-skewed, with most tracts below about $500,000 and a few far above it. Equal interval classes put `r n_eq[1]` of the `r length(x)` tracts in the lowest class, so most of the county looks the same and only a handful of very expensive tracts stand out. Quantile classes put about `r round(length(x) / 5)` tracts in each class, which shows the differences across the whole county. The cost is that the top class stretches from `r paste0("$", fmt(br_q[5]))` to `r paste0("$", fmt(br_q[6]))`. For showing where homes are least affordable, the quantile map is the better choice, as long as the legend makes the wide top class clear.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#### both partners ####
meck <- acs_tract_nc |> filter(COUNTYFP == "119")

ggplot(meck, aes(x = med_house_val)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50000, fill = "lightgrey", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Median home value ($)", y = "Number of tracts")

#### Partner A: equal interval ####
tm_shape(meck) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "med_house_val",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5, values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"))

#breaks and counts (classInt is installed with tmap)
breaks_eq <- classInt::classIntervals(na.omit(meck$med_house_val), n = 5, style = "equal")$brks
table(cut(meck$med_house_val, breaks_eq, include.lowest = TRUE))

tm_shape(meck) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "med_house_val", fill_alpha = 0.6,
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5, values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Median home value ($)")) +
  tm_title("Median home value, Mecklenburg County (equal interval)") +
  tm_basemap("CartoDB.PositronNoLabels")

#### Partner B: quantile ####
tm_shape(meck) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "med_house_val",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"))

breaks_q <- classInt::classIntervals(na.omit(meck$med_house_val), n = 5, style = "quantile")$brks
table(cut(meck$med_house_val, breaks_q, include.lowest = TRUE))

tm_shape(meck) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "med_house_val", fill_alpha = 0.6,
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Median home value ($)")) +
  tm_title("Median home value, Mecklenburg County (quantile)") +
  tm_basemap("CartoDB.PositronNoLabels")
```
